questions.stem: A 24-year-old man attended outpatient clinic for initiation of ART after a recent diagnosis of HIV infection. He was keen to get started on treatment. Investigations: CD4 count 450 cells/μ L HIV RNA 120,000 copies/mL No baseline resistance demonstrated on HIV genotyping HLA B*5701 negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antiretroviral regimen?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine + boosted darunavir Rilpivirine is not recommended in patients who have a HIV RNA >100,000 copies/mL or CD 4 T cell count <200 cells/μL at the start of treatment. Similarly abacavir is only recommended for treatment in patients with HIV RNA >100,000 copies/per mL if it is combined with dolutegravir. In practice INSTI-based regimens are preferred and NNRTI-based regimens are now considered alternative. However if an INSTI cannot be used then boosted darunavir, rilpivirine or efavirenz can be considered in combination with TDF or TAF .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q35

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of myalgia of the lower extremities spreading proximally, increased fatigue, and polyuria. He was known to be HIVpositive, on treatment with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/ emtricitabine + raltegravir for the past year. Investigations: Sodium 135 mmol/L Potassium 2.0 mmol/L Glucose 90 mg/dl Chloride 107 mmol/L Bicarbonate 17 mEq/L Phosphorus 1.4 mg/dl Creatinine kinase 2015 U/L Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (previous baseline 1.2 mg/dL) Urinalysis: protein 30 mg/d and glucose 500 mg/dL Baseline genotype prior to initiating ART did not demonstrate resistance HLA B*5701 negative HBsAg positive
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?
questions.explanation: Abacavir/lamivudine/dolutegravir + entecavir The presence of a hyperchloremic nonanion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, glucosuria, and proteinuria suggest that this patient has tenofovir-induced Fanconi’s syndrome; therefore tenofovir should be discontinued. Although raltegravir has been associated with rhabdomyolysis the other laboratory findings are suggestive of Fanconi’s syndrome. This patient has hepatitis B co-infection, and therefore an optimal treatment regimen should cover both viruses. Discontinuation of agents with anti-HBV activity can result in serious hepatocellular damage following reactivation of HBV . Lamivudine has activity against HBV; however, resistance develops quickly, and therefore dual therapy is recommended.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q36

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man attended for review. He was known to have hypertension, chronic hepatitis B, and HIV . He had been started 3 months earlier on lisinopril 10 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg daily as he had an elevated Framingham risk score due to elevated blood pressure and hypercholesterolemia. He was also taking hydrochlorothiazide, aspirin, multivitamins, and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide fumarate. Investigations: CD4 count 756 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable 3 Months Earlier Current Visit Total cholesterol (mg/dL) 315 200 LDL (mg/dL) 197 80 HDL (mg/dL) 30 35 Triglycerides (mg/dL) 378 215 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 0.9 1.1 Alkaline phosphatase (U/L) 45 46 ALT 34 116 AST 30 205
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of the new onset hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Drug–drug interaction with statin This patient is suffering from a drug–drug interaction from being on an antiretroviral therapy regimen with cobicistat and initiation of a statin. Because of the association of HIV with dyslipidemia, it is recommended to screen all new patients for hyperlipidemia at their first HIV Clinic appointment. If hyperlipidemia is found, then statins should be initiated, and lipid panels should be monitored within 1–3 months and then every 6–12 months thereafter. However, guidelines for initiation of a cholesterol-lowering agent are the same as the general population for persons living with HIV . It is contraindicated to start statins metabolized by CYP3A in patients on protease inhibitors, including simvastatin and lovastatin. For patients on a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor regimen, it is recommended to start pitavastatin and, for patients on all other regimens, it is recommended to start atorvastatin at 10 mg daily. A lower dose is recommended because atorvastatin is partially metabolized by CYP3A. Pravastatin is not recommended any longer, because it is not as potent as the other two mentioned above. Now with the advent of antiretroviral regimens containing cobicistat, which is also an inhibitor of CYP 3A4, it is also contraindicated to initiate statins that are highly metabolized by CYP3A. While rosuvastatin is not metabolized by CYP3A4, five- to sevenfold increases in rosuvastatin levels are seen when co-administered with a boosted protease-inhibitor regimen or a regimen including cobicistat; therefore it is recommended to start rosuvastatin at a lower dose of 10 mg daily. Hepatitis B co-infection can be adequately treated with tenofovir alafenamide with no resistance seen in studies where patients are compliant. Therefore this patient should not be developing transaminitis due to viral hepatitis. A hepatitis D superinfection is possible, but unlikely. Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune disease of the small intralobular bile ducts that characteristically leads to drastic elevation in alkaline phosphatase levels, which was not seen in this case. However, there are biliary tract disorders that are more common among persons living with HIV , including acalculous cholecystitis and AIDS cholangiopathy. ACE-I are not known to cause hepatic impairment. In patients with renal impairment, decreased elimination of ACE-I can be seen leading to increased serum creatinine levels.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of increased abdominal weight gain and generalized muscle weakness. She had been found to have HIV 8 years previously when she was diagnosed in pregnancy. She was initially treated with zidovudine/lamivudine and lopinavir/ ritonavir during pregnancy and continued it until the previous year when she switched to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine/cobicistat/elvitegravir for ART simplification. She also had a history of seasonal allergies and a sporting injury to her right knee. In addition to ART , she was taking OTC antihistamines, intranasal fluticasone spray, and ibuprofen.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toxicity from nasal spray Cases of iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome have been reported in patients who are co-administered antiretroviral boosting agents ritonavir or cobicistat with cytochrome 3A metabolized corticosteroids. This can include inhaled, intranasal, and intraarticular corticosteroids, which the patient may be acquiring over the counter or from other providers.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q38

questions.lead_in: The K103N mutation confers resistance to which of the following antiretroviral medications?
questions.explanation: Efavirenz K103N is the most common mutation associated with efavirenz resistance. This mutation also confers resistance to delavirdine and nevirapine, but not rilpivirine and etravirine.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q46

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman attended outpatient clinic having recently moved to the United States from Zimbabwe. She was not on antiretroviral therapy but reported receiving ART during delivery of her first child and antenatally during her second pregnancy. Investigations: CD4 count 370 cells/μL HIV viral load 36,000 copies/mL HIV genotype: Y181C mutation detected
questions.lead_in: What antiretroviral agent is contraindicated with this mutation?
questions.explanation: Nevirapine Y181C is selected in patients treated with nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. It is the signature mutation for nevirapine and causes high-level reduction in nevirapine susceptibility, intermediate-level reduction in rilpivirine and etravirine susceptibility, and low-level reduction in efavirenz susceptibility.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q21

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man was admitted with a 6-week history of cough, fatigue, ∼10 lb weight loss, night sweats, and fever. He had recently been diagnosed with HIV . He had been born in Thailand but moved to the United States 10 years ago. He had been in prison for 2 years and was PPD negative at that time. Investigations: CD4 count 312/μL HIV VL 385, 000 copies /mL CXR: left upper lobe infiltrates Sputum microscopy: abundant acid-fast bacilli seen; Xpert MTB/RIF positive for both MTB and an rpo B gene mutation MDR-TB was suspected; it was thought that he would need between five and seven active antituberculosis drugs during the initiation phase.
questions.lead_in: What would be the best course of action?

options.text: Defer TB treatment for 2 weeks and start ART now
Start ART within 2 weeks and start TB treatment now
Start both TB and ART treatment now
Start TB treatment now and defer ART for 2–8 weeks
Start TB treatment now plus steroids and defer ART for 2–8 weeks

questions.explanation: Start TB treatment now and defer ART for 2–8 weeks Tuberculosis treatment should always be started once the clinician determines the diagnosis. In HIV-TB co-infection, ART should be initiated within 2 weeks only if CD4 count is <50/μL. In all other cases with CD4 count ≥50 initiation of ART should be started within 8 weeks, with exception of TB involving the CNS, where ART should be delayed for the first 8 weeks.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q17

questions.stem: A 48-year-old presented with extensive bruising on his left thigh after a minor injury 2 days earlier. Two weeks previously he had been started on rivaroxaban for a pulmonary thromboembolism and right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis. He was known to have well-controlled HIV , treated with elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir/ emtricitabine.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his hematoma?
questions.explanation: Drug interaction This patient is suffering from a drug–drug interaction between his rivaroxaban and the cobicistat in his antiretroviral therapy. Cobicistat is an inhibitor of CYP 3A4 and would lead to higher plasma concentrations of the rivaroxaban, which could lead to hemorrhagic events. Therefore, it is not recommended to start rivaroxaban in patients on an ART regimen with cobicistat. Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) is considered an AIDS-defining illness and is typically seen in patients with advanced disease (CD4 cell count <100 cells/ μL). Primary CNS lymphoma and primary effusion lymphoma may also be seen in patients with advanced disease. The most common NHL seen in patients with HIV is B-cell lymphoma, followed by Burkett’s lymphoma. Plasmablastic lymphomas are rare but are also more common in people with HIV . The clinical presentation is also not characteristic, with no B-type symptoms, growing masses, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. This patient does not have any other clinical features suggesting a thrombotic microangiopathy, thrombocytopenic purpura, or hemolytic uremic syndrome with signs of systemic organ dysfunction, which are all more common in patients infected with HIV . Protein C and S deficiencies are usually seen in patients with advanced disease and co-infection with an opportunistic infection. Protein C and S deficiency usually result in hypercoagulability manifesting as venous thromboembolism or arterial thrombosis. There have been case reports of patients developing warfarin-induced skin necrosis with protein C and S deficiency. Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder. Mild type 1 WBD may well manifest later in life when uncovered by antiplatelet medications; however, type 3 WBD usually presents in infancy or early childhood with bleeding provoked by minor trauma.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q19

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man attended for routine follow-up. He had HIV treated with tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine + twice-daily raltegravir. He had been diagnosed with a peptic ulcer and had started taking lansoprazole. His brother had recently died from a drug overdose, and the patient had been drinking alcohol heavily in response. As a result he was finding it difficult to remember to take his medication. Investigations: 2 Weeks Before Clinic Day of Clinic CD4 count / μL 395 HIV RNA copies/ml 2050 3950 HIV resistance assay Q148R mutation detected
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antiretroviral regimen?

options.text: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine + atazanavir/ cobicistat once daily
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine + ritonavir boosted darunavir once daily

questions.explanation: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine + ritonavir boosted darunavir once daily Q148R is a mutation that reduced susceptibility to both raltegravir and elvitegravir. Alone, there is evidence that Q148R confers low-level resistance to dolutegravir, and therefore if dolutegravir is used it should be dosed twice daily. Co-administration of atazanavir with a proton pump inhibitor is not recommended.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old Senegalese man was found to have HIV on routine screening with a fourth-generation combined p24 Ag/Ab ELISA. A confirmatory test with a second-generation ELISA for IgG to differentiate between HIV-1 and HIV-2 infection detected HIV-2 antibodies. He was negative for HIV-1 antibodies and an HIV-1 RNA viral load was negative. An HIV-2 RNA viral load was sent to the reference laboratory. His CD4 count was 458 cells/μL (mm3).
questions.lead_in: What class of antiretrovirals is HIV-2 intrinsically resistant to?
questions.explanation: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors The NNRTI binding pocket is structurally different in HIV-2, conferring innate resistance onto this class of drugs. They should not be used in the treatment of HIV-2.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q47

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man attended the sexual health clinic following partner notification for gonorrhea. He was screened for rectal, urethral, and pharyngeal gonorrhea and chlamydia, and had epidemiologic treatment for gonorrhea with intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin. Given his high-risk sexual behavior (>30 partners in the preceding 3 months, unprotected insertive and receptive anal sex, participation in chemsex parties) he requested a point of care HIV test. This was positive, and a laboratory sample confirmed HIV and hepatitis C infection. CD4 count was 525 cells/μL, HIV viral load 12,458 copies/mL. Treatment was recommended given his co-infection status and as he wanted to reduce the risk of transmission to partners. A baseline HIV resistance screen was obtained prior to starting Atripla (tenofovir, emtricitabine, efavirenz).
questions.lead_in: What mutation in his resistance test would predict likely treatment failure with efavirenz?
questions.explanation: Y181C Amino acid substitutions such as K103N or Y181C prevent NNRTIs binding.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q48

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fever, sore throat, and a rash. On examination she had a maculopapular rash and generalized lymphadenopathy. Investigations: Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL AST 65 units/L ALT 96 units/L Bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL EBV IgM positive, IgG positive, EBNA positive HIV Ab/Ag test negative HIV viral load 1.2 million copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine +atazanavir/ cobicistat Initiation of ART in symptomatic acute HIV reduces symptoms and is now recommended. As a HLA B*5701 result is not available, abacavir-based regimens should be avoided. In the setting of acute infection, resistance assays may not be readily available, as in this case. In the absence of a resistance assay a protease-based or dolutegravir-based regimen is recommended pending results. Tenofovir alafenamide+cobicis tat+elvitegravir is incorrect as it is an incomplete regimen.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q21

questions.lead_in: Hypersensitivity to what drug can be predicted by HLAB*5701 testing?
questions.explanation: Abacavir Abacavir hypersensitivity can be predicted by testing for the HLAB*5701 allele. The syndrome can be life-threatening and can manifest with fever and other constitutional symptoms, rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, and dyspnea.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q44

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman attended for review after a positive pregnancy test. She was known to have HIV and was taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine/efavirenz. She reported ongoing compliance with her medication. She estimated that she was 7 weeks pregnant. Investigations: CD4 count 550 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Advise her to consider termination due to the risk of teratogenicity
Continue current ART and routine monitoring
Stop ART and recommence during the 2nd trimester
Switch to ritonavir-boosted darunavir, zidovudine, and emtricitabine

questions.explanation: Continue current ART and routine monitoring HIV-infected pregnant women established on ART who present for care during the 1st trimester should continue treatment during pregnancy, provided the regimen is tolerated and effective in suppressing viral replication. Women who become pregnant on efavirenz-containing regimens who are virally suppressed and tolerating it should continue their current regimens. In the past efavirenz was linked with teratogenicity based on animal studies; however, increased teratogenicity has not been seen in the babies of mothers exposed to efavirenz in the 1st trimester in registry studies and meta-analyses. Therefore guidelines recommend continuing treatment: http://aidsinfo.nih.gov/contentfiles/lvgu idelines/PerinatalGL.pd. There is no data on cobicistat in pregnancy, therefore for present protease inhibitors should be ritonavir-boosted.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q34

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman was reviewed with a new diagnosis of HIV and hepatitis B co-infection. A pregnancy test was negative. Despite multiple educational meetings she declined HIV treatment but was interested in hepatitis B treatment. Investigations: AST 89 IU/L ALT 98 units/L CD4 count 434 cells/μL HIV viral load 55,000 copies/mL HBsAg positive HBV viral load 540,000 IU/mL Liver biopsy showed significant fibrosis but no cirrhosis
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to offer?
questions.explanation: Peginterferon alfa 2B The patient is refusing HIV treatment at this time. The concern is that using an agent for her hepatitis that also has activity against HIV would lead to the development of HIV resistance. Entecavir, lamivudine, tenofovir, and emtricitabine are all active against both HIV and HBV . Only peginterferon alfa 2B alone will not lead to HIV-resistance. Remember that interferon therapy has many disadvantages, multiple side effects (i.e., influenza-like syndrome, myalgias, depression, fatigue, etc.) and is only given IM. If the patient would have accepted treatment for both HIV and HBV , then combination therapy with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir would have been the optimal choice. This regimen offers three active drugs against HIV as recommended by the DHHS guidelines and at the same time would offer two active drugs against hepatitis B (tenofovir and emtricitabine).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q8

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman from Zimbabwe presented with a 2-week history of increasing confusion, ataxia, headache, and fevers. She was admitted and a lumbar puncture performed after a CT scan of her head. Investigations: HIV-1 Ag/Ab positive CD4 5 cells/μL HIV viral load 225 000 copies/mL Serum CRAG positive CSF: opening pressure 450 mmH2O (120–250) Protein 0.9 g/L (0.15–0.45) Glucose 2.3 mmol/L (plasma glucose 7.2) White blood cells 0.05 ×109/L(50/mm3), 90% lymphocytes Cryptococcal antigen positive CSF cultures: growth on Sab plates consistent with Cryptococcus neoformans She was started on liposomal amphotericin B and 5-flucytosine.

When her serum CRAG becomes negative

It is generally recommended to delay ART initiation to at least 4 weeks after start of antifungal therapy to avoid severe immune reconstitution syndrome.

parts.text: Abacavir (NRTI)
Efavirenz (NNRTI)
Atazanavir (PI)
Tenofovir (NRTI)
Elvitegravir-cobicistat (boosted INSTI)

cohort_answer.text: Abacavir: HLA B5701+ (hypersensitivity reaction). Efavirenz: Psychiatric conditions; Pregnant/planning pregnancy (neural tube defect association in non-human primates). parts.text: Give three first-line regimens recommended by guidelines
In general, what are the indications to start antiretroviral therapy?

cohort_answer.text:
K103N and Y181C mutations confer resistance to Efavirenz and Nevirapine. M184V mutation – decreases susceptibility to FTC / 3TC but increases susceptibility to TDF, usually first mutation to appear
Indications to start ART: All HIV positive individuals regardless of CD4 count. START and TEMPRANO trials were associated with decreased mortality when ARVs were started when CD4 counts >500. Delayed ART: crypto (2-10 weeks after starting tx), TB (CD4>50, start within 8 weeks)

questions.question: HIV with CD4 of 550.

parts.text: Please provide 4 benefits to start HIV therapy.
HLA test is pending, name two potential regimens to start the patient on.
Four indications for resistance setting.

questions.model_answer: a) Benefits of early ART (4): (1) Reduces AIDS-defining and non-AIDS-defining morbidity/mortality (START trial). (2) Reduces risk of HIV transmission to partners (treatment as prevention). (3) Preserves/restores immune function, reduces immune activation. (4) Reduces risk of non-AIDS complications (cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, malignancy) associated with untreated HIV. b) Two regimens (HLA-B5701 pending, avoid abacavir until result back): (1) Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (BIC/TAF/FTC). (2) Dolutegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine (DTG + TDF or TAF/FTC). c) Four indications for resistance testing: (1) Prior to starting ART (baseline, treatment-naive). (2) Virologic failure on current regimen. (3) Pregnancy, prior to starting ART. (4) Suboptimal viral load suppression / suspected transmitted resistance.

parts.text: HIV with CD4 of 550, name trial supporting initiation of ARVs with CD4 >500.

questions.model_answer: START trial (INSIGHT START Study Group, NEJM 2015): randomized trial of immediate vs deferred ART in ART-naive patients with CD4 >500 cells/µL; showed immediate initiation significantly reduced serious AIDS-related and non-AIDS-related events, establishing benefit of starting ART regardless of CD4 count.

questions.question: Patient would like a one tablet per day regiment, he is HLA negative.

parts.text: Please name 4 potential regimens.
Which of the four above would you give in the patient if he has DM2 and renal failure?

questions.model_answer: a) Four one-pill-daily regimens: (1) Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (Biktarvy). (2) Dolutegravir/lamivudine (Dovato). (3) Dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine (Triumeq) - only if HLA-B5701 negative. (4) Elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (Genvoya). b) With T2DM and renal impairment: avoid TDF-containing and abacavir/renal-adjusted regimens; preferred is bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine (Biktarvy) as TAF has less nephrotoxicity than TDF; dolutegravir/lamivudine not preferred if renal impairment limits lamivudine dosing flexibility, but Biktarvy is single tablet and safe down to eGFR ≥30.

cohort_answer.text: 4 benefits: Decreased mortality; Decreased morbidity from infections (particularly tuberculosis), malignancies (START and TEMPRANO trial); Reduced transmission; Appears to increase probability of restoring normal CD4 counts, normal CD4/CD8 ratio, and lower levels of immune activation/inflammation; Slows disease progression. Two potential regimens with HLA pending: not documented. Four indications for resistance testing: For all patients at entry into care to guide selection of ARTs; Prior to initiation of ARVs if there has been a delay since initial resistance testing done upon entry into care; Prior to change in drug regimen in patients with virologic failure and HIV RNA >1,000 copies/mL, suboptimal viral load reduction, or HIV RNA levels >500 but <1,000 copies/mL (may be unsuccessful but should still be considered). Trial: ART-START and TEMPRANO trials. Four one-tablet-per-day regimens: BIC/TAF/FTC; DTG/ABC/3TC; DRV/c/TAF/FTC; RPV/TAF/FTC; RPV/TDF/FTC (https://aidsinfo.nih.gov/guidelines/html/1/adult-and-adolescent-arv/11/what-to-start). With DM2 and renal failure (CKD: avoid TDF unless has ESRD, use ABC or TAF): DTG/ABC/3TC or BIC/TAF/FTC

parts.text: List three ARV regimens that she can start that will not require her to change rifampin.
When should she start her ARV treatment if her CD4 count is 20?
When should she start her ARV treatment if her CD4 count is 85?

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: EFV 600mg daily + TDF/FTC; Dolutegravir 50mg BID + TDF/FTC; Raltegravir 400mg BID + TDF/FTC. CD4 20: start ARV within 2 weeks (higher IRIS risk but lower mortality). CD4 85: start between 2-8 weeks (lower IRIS risk by delaying)

parts.text: Name 3 drugs you could use in a regimen with a TDF/FTC backbone and the dosing regimen (i.e. give the third drug name and dosing)
When should you start ART in this patient?

questions.model_answer: a) Third agent options with TDF/FTC backbone when rifampin must be continued (rifampin induces CYP3A4, lowering levels of most ART): (1) Raltegravir 800 mg PO BID (double standard dose). (2) Dolutegravir 50 mg PO BID (double standard dose) instead of daily. (3) Efavirenz 600 mg PO daily (standard dose, minimal interaction with rifampin). b) Start ART within 2 weeks of starting TB treatment given CD4 <50, accepting higher risk of IRIS, because of high early mortality risk with very low CD4.

Dolutegravir plus (emtricitabine/lamivudine) plus TAF/TDF (AI). Dolutegravir/lamivudine (AI) - NOT if RNA >500,000 copies/mL, HBV, no genotype. Raltegravir plus (emtricitabine or lamivudine) plus (TAF/TDF) (BI/BII).

parts.text: What are the components of the injectable agent?
Name the classes of the components

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action of TAF?
What is the reason that TAF can be given at a lower dose than tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)?
What are the two side effects of TDF that are reduced in TAF?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action of TAF: TAF is a prodrug of tenofovir; after cellular uptake it is hydrolyzed to tenofovir and then phosphorylated to tenofovir diphosphate, which is incorporated into the growing HIV DNA chain by reverse transcriptase, causing chain termination (same active moiety and mechanism as TDF).
b) Reason TAF can be dosed lower than TDF: TAF is more stable in plasma and is preferentially hydrolyzed intracellularly (in lymphoid cells), resulting in higher intracellular concentrations of active tenofovir diphosphate but markedly lower plasma tenofovir concentrations compared to TDF, so a much lower dose achieves equivalent/greater antiviral activity with less systemic drug exposure.
c) Two TDF side effects reduced with TAF: (1) nephrotoxicity/renal tubular dysfunction, (2) decreased bone mineral density.

questions.question: NRTI-induced lactic acidosis

parts.text: Recognition and management (esp choice of future ART)

cohort_answer.text: Hyperlactatemia and lactic acidosis associated with NRTI use, typically without systemic hypoperfusion (type B lactic acidosis). questions.question: HIV resistance testing

parts.text: Define phenotypic vs genotypic?

cohort_answer.text: Genotypic test detects drug resistance mutations in relevant genes. Requires VL>500-1000. TAT 1-2 weeks. Increased sensitivity over phenotypic for detecting wild type and resistance. Reduced costs. Preferred. Phenotypic testing: measures ability of virus to grow in different concentrations of ARV drug. TAT 2-3 weeks. More expensive than genotypic

questions.question: Q27 (2008, 2012 AM) Maraviroc

parts.text: a) Class and MOA

cohort_answer.text: a) Entry/CCR5 inhibitor; inhibits binding of HIV gp120 to CCR5 co-receptor by binding CCR5 and changing conformation. b) Common: postural hypotension, anaemia, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, loss of appetite, flatulence, weakness, depression, insomnia, raised liver enzymes, rash. parts.text: What is the mechanism of action
Why can use at lower dose than TDF
Which side effects better in TAF vs TDF

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor - prevents HIV from replicating by competitively inhibiting reverse transcriptase enzyme and preventing DNA production (NNRTI works similarly but via noncompetitive inhibition). questions.question: HIV patient with CD4 62, viral load 250K. Immune HBV serology. Infection with PJP.

parts.text: When to start ARVs? And why?
Give 6 screening tests indicated as part of her initial HIV assessment?

cohort_answer.text:
When to start ARVs: ASAP, within 2 weeks of dx of PCP – associated with lower death. In an RCT of 282 patients with OIs other than TB, 63% of whom had definite or presumptive PCP, a significantly lower incidence of AIDS progression or death (a secondary study endpoint) was seen in subjects randomized to early (median 12 days after initiation of therapy for OI) versus deferred initiation of ART (median 45 days). Six screening tests: Hep C serology; Baseline labs: CBC, LFTs, renal function; Cryptococcal antigen serum; TST / IGRA; Syphilis Screening; Gonorrhea and Chlamydia screen; HPV; VZV if no clear history of chicken pox +/- immunization; Toxo; G6PD screen (in case can't use TMP-SMX); Hep A (more in MSM)

a) Four risk factors for increased HIV transmission risk after a percutaneous exposure: (1) deep puncture/injury. (2) Visible blood on the injuring device. d) Duration of PEP: 28 days.

questions.question: New diagnosis HIV in pregnant woman from Africa at 36 weeks gestation. Viral load 78k, resistance testing and HLA-B*5701 pending.

parts.text: What are three art regimens to start, and when would you start each?
She has a stat viral load at delivery showing viral load 2700. What management do you recommend for her delivery?
The baby is born. What regimen do you prescribe for baby and for how long?
What is Canada’s recommendation regarding infant feeding? Give two reasons why.

questions.model_answer:
a) Three ART regimens and timing: (1) Dolutegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine (or lamivudine) - preferred, start immediately/as soon as possible given high viral load and late gestation, no need to await resistance/HLA results (avoid abacavir until HLA-B*5701 negative); (2) Raltegravir-based regimen with tenofovir/emtricitabine - alternative if DTG unavailable/contraindicated, start immediately; (3) Boosted darunavir/ritonavir + tenofovir/emtricitabine - alternative PI-based option, also start immediately given proximity to delivery and high viral load, as PI regimens have long safety track record in pregnancy.
b) Delivery management with VL 2700 near term: recommend intravenous zidovudine intrapartum (VL >1000 copies/mL near delivery) and scheduled Cesarean section at 38 weeks to reduce risk of perinatal transmission.
c) Infant regimen: given maternal viraemia at delivery, infant is at increased transmission risk - give infant combination ART prophylaxis (e.g., zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir/nevirapine) for 6 weeks rather than zidovudine monotherapy.
d) Canada's recommendation on infant feeding: formula feeding (replacement feeding) is recommended rather than breastfeeding when the mother's viral load is not confirmed suppressed. Two reasons: (1) risk of postnatal HIV transmission through breast milk even with maternal ART, particularly with detectable/unknown viral load near delivery; (2) safe, affordable replacement feeding (formula) is readily available in Canada, removing the rationale for accepting transmission risk that exists in resource-limited settings.

questions.question: Newly diagnosed HIV, CD4 of 7 and viral load >500,000 started on Triumeq. Now has fever, seizure and decreased LOC. You suspected IRIS.

parts.text: Describe IRIS
Name 2 risk factors for IRIS
List 4 pathogens that can explain her presentation
What would you use to treat her IRIS

cohort_answer.text: IRIS description: An exaggerated inflammatory reaction to a disease-causing organism that may occur during immune reconstitution (recovery) following initiation of ARVs. Two forms occur: 'unmasking' IRIS where new symptoms of an undiagnosed infection appear, and 'paradoxical' IRIS, where a previously treated infection worsens after ARV therapy is started (https://clinicalinfo.hiv.gov/en/glossary/immune-reconstitution-inflammatory-syndrome-iris). Risk factors: Low CD4 count (<100); High Viral Load (early initiation of ARV before treatment of infection). Pathogens: Cryptococcus neoformans; JCV (PML-IRIS); Mycobacterium Tuberculosis; Toxoplasma; MAC; CMV (immune recovery uveitis). Treatment: 0.5-1mg/kg/day Prednisone equivalent as Dexamethasone, tapered over 2-6 weeks depending on clinical improvement (IDSA Cryptococcus 2010)

questions.question: You see a patient with a new diagnosis of HIV infection and pneumocystis pneumonia. They are requiring 4 L/min of supplemental oxygen to maintain their oxygen saturation >90%.

parts.text: The patient reports a history of full-body rash (but no mucous membrane involvement) to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 years ago. List FOUR alternate antibiotic or management options.
How soon should you start antiretroviral therapy?
List TWO criteria you should follow to discontinue prophylaxis for pneumocystis pneumonia.

questions.model_answer: a) Four alternatives to TMP-SMX (non-anaphylactic rash history, moderate-severe PJP requiring steroids given hypoxemia): (1) IV pentamidine. (2) Clindamycin plus primaquine (check G6PD first). (3) Consider TMP-SMX desensitization if clinically feasible given it remains most effective. (4) Atovaquone is an option but reserved for mild-moderate disease, not appropriate alone here given hypoxemia (4 L O2, moderate-severe disease); adjunctive corticosteroids required regardless of antibiotic choice given room air-equivalent hypoxemia (PaO2 <70 or A-a gradient >35). b) ART timing: start within 2 weeks of PJP diagnosis/treatment initiation (early ART improves survival, per ACTG 5164). c) Criteria to discontinue secondary PJP prophylaxis: CD4 count >200 cells/µL for at least 3 months on ART with sustained virologic suppression (undetectable viral load).

questions.question: You have a mother in clinic who is 38-weeks pregnant who is otherwise healthy. She has been on Biktarvy for her entire pregnancy and is virologically suppressed. She is interested in breastfeeding.

parts.text: Based on the Canadian Pediatric & Perinatal HIV/AIDS Research group consensus recommendations for infant feeding in HIV, what are THREE criteria to proceed with breast feeding?

questions.model_answer: Three criteria per Canadian Perinatal HIV/AIDS Research group consensus to proceed with breastfeeding: (1) maternal HIV RNA suppressed (<50 copies/mL) throughout pregnancy and confirmed near delivery/postpartum; (2) mother is engaged in ongoing HIV care and committed to strict ART adherence, with close monitoring of maternal and infant HIV status throughout breastfeeding; (3) informed, shared decision-making has occurred with counselling on the residual (very low but not zero) risk of transmission, and infant receives appropriate postnatal ARV prophylaxis with regular follow-up testing.

questions.question: HIV + patient co-infected with Hepatitis B. Doing well on ARVs in terms of CD4 and VL but LFTs are increasing as is the Hep B viral load. In addition, he has very high lipids that have not responded to diet and exercise.

parts.text: How would you change his therapy, justify your decision?

cohort_answer.text: If on lamivudine monotherapy: TDF or TAF should be added; avoid others like emtricitabine (cross resistance to lamivudine) or entecavir (partial cross-resistance if lamivudine resistance+). If on tenofovir or entecavir: check adherence, resistance profile, drug interactions (no known tenofovir resistance mutations). For cirrhotic patients, add a second agent (e.g. entecavir to tenofovir). Avoid PIs – high risk for increased lipids, CV risk. Also avoid ABC – high risk CV

parts.text: 2 strategies to decrease the risk of HIV transmission to baby
2 strategies to decrease risk of HBV transmission to baby?

cohort_answer.text: A) Start ART asap; IV ZDV during labor and until delivery if VL>1000; avoid invasive procedures; consider CS if VL>1000; start PEP for baby (ZDV+NVP+3TC x6 weeks); avoid breastfeeding. B) Maternal antiviral tx; HBIg at birth (within 12h); HepB vaccine at birth (within 12h) followed by dose 2 and 3 at 1 and 6 months respectively.

Patient with compensated cirrhosis, Genotype 1a Hep C. Needs treatment. Has HIV on truvada/efavirenz.

parts.text: Last question - what is viral test needed if patient to start simeprevir/sofosbuvir.

cohort_answer.text: Check for Q80K polymorphism, confers low level resistance to in vitro simeprevir activity. If the patient is NON-CIRRHOTIC -> this does not matter. Can treat for 12 weeks. If the patient is CIRRHOTIC and Q80K polymorphism present, consider a different regimen. As a rule -> if patient has cirrhosis, we have to check for resistance. If the patient is not cirrhotic resistance testing is not usually needed.

questions.question: A patient with HIV is pregnant. She is not on treatment:

parts.text: Name 3 antiretroviral regimens and when would you start them?
b. What 2 recommendations do you have for the mother at delivery?
c. What regimen for the baby and timing?
d. When would you test the baby?
e. 2 current Canadian recommendations for feeding?

cohort_answer.text: a) Dolutegravir/Abacavir/Lamivudine; TAF/Emtricitabine plus dolutegravir (or TDF); TAF/Emtricitabine plus Darunavir/ritonavir (or TDF, better studied). Start ASAP. b) VL>1000: C-section at 38 weeks and intrapartum zidovudine. VL<1000: delivery mode determined by OB, consider intrapartum zidovudine. Avoid artificial rupture of membranes, forceps/vacuum extractor, fetal scalp electrodes. c) Presumptive therapy at birth with Zidovudine, lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir. d) HIV NAT at birth and 6 weeks. e) Exclusive formula; no mixed feeding (solid/liquid foods prior to 6 months increases HIV transmission risk).
